title: Trump blasts Supreme Court on social media
author: Amy Howe
content:
Skip to main content

Newsletter

Sep 16, 2026

Today, SCOTUSblog and Johns Hopkins University are coming together to preview the cases and questions that will shape the 2026-27 Supreme Court term. This event, which is presented by Cooley, will include a keynote address featuring Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL) and Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA); a live taping of the Advisory Opinions podcast; a fireside chat with Cooley partner and former U.S. Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar; and a panel with Brett Gerry (chief legal officer of Boeing), Brian Callanan (general counsel of TD Bank U.S.), and Jeff Taylor (general counsel of ExxonMobil). Tomorrow’s newsletter will include a brief overview of the event.

At the Court

The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to clear the way for it to use the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements database to identify noncitizens on state voter rolls. On Tuesday, the groups challenging this plan filed a response to the administration’s request. For more on the dispute, see the On Site section below.

Morning Reads

Trump calls Supreme Court mail ballot ruling ‘big loss for Republicans’

Dan Mangan, CNBC

In a Tuesday morning post on Truth Social, President Donald Trump “blasted the Supreme Court for blocking a new controversial U.S. Postal Service rule on mail-in ballots from being used for the upcoming midterm elections,” according to CNBC. “It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do,” the president wrote. In the post, “Trump also harshly criticized his three Supreme Court appointees,” Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett, “for apparently joining with all three liberal justices, plus Chief Justice John Roberts,” in Monday’s decision. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” he wrote.

Todd Blanche: Supreme Court setback on mail-in ballots won’t stop election integrity efforts

Tom Howell Jr., The Washington Times

During a Tuesday press briefing, Attorney General Todd Blanche asserted that “efforts to tighten rules around mail-in voting will continue beyond November despite the Supreme Court’s refusal to step in and revive President Trump’s plan to police mail-in ballots for the midterm elections,” according to The Washington Times. “We’re not going to stop the work that we’re doing, but we are of course going to follow the orders of the court,” Blanche said, adding that the Supreme Court’s decision “doesn’t affect ongoing criminal investigations into illegal voting.” Blanche also addressed Trump’s complaints about the Supreme Court on social media. “He is very frustrated,” Blanche told reporters. “He has every right, and indeed he should, communicate his concerns with the Supreme Court whenever he has them. This isn’t the first time he’s done it, and it won’t be the last.”

John Eastman asks US Supreme Court to undo disbarment over Trump election efforts

David Thomas, Reuters

Conservative attorney John Eastman has filed a petition for review with the Supreme Court, asking the justices “to reinstate his California law license after he was disbarred in the state earlier this year over his efforts to overturn Republican President Donald Trump’s 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden,” according to Reuters. In the petition, Eastman contends “his legal advocacy was protected by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, and that he was disciplined in a ‘politicized’ bar proceeding. He said other attorneys who took part in legal proceedings that sought to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election were not disciplined.” Reuters noted that “[i]t is rare for the U.S. Supreme Court to weigh in on attorney disciplinary cases, which are normally decided by the top court of respective states.”

EPA rollback may worsen Trump’s Supreme Court climate headache

Lesley Clark, Politico

On Oct. 5, Trump “administration attorneys will appear alongside oil companies at the Supreme Court to argue that the justices should put the kibosh on dozens of state court lawsuits that – if successful – would force companies like ExxonMobil, Chevron and Suncor Energy to pay billions of dollars for contributing to climate change,” according to Politico. In its filings in that case, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, the Justice Department has contended “that EPA – not the states and cities behind the climate lawsuits against oil producers – is the primary regulator of greenhouse gases.” However, legal experts who spoke with Politico believe that claim is in tension with “[t]he Trump administration’s move on Monday to undo EPA climate rules” for power plants and its broader effort to reduce EPA’s involvement in climate issues. For its part, the “DOJ has said it does not see any conflict with its decision to rescind climate rules and its Supreme Court argument that state-level climate lawsuits interfere with the federal government’s job.”

In Fits and Starts, the Supreme Court Stands Up to Trump

Adam Liptak, The New York Times

In an analysis for The New York Times, Adam Liptak explored the Supreme Court’s evolving relationship with the Trump administration, noting that, for much of President Donald Trump’s second term, “the court seemed to have settled on a strategy of deference, ducking and delay.” “But sometimes,” Liptak continued, “the court put its foot down,” including on Monday in the mail-in voting dispute. “The majority opinion about mail-in balloting on Monday was just three sentences long, but it went further than it might have. Instead of ruling merely that the administration’s plan had been rolled out too close to the November election, a conclusion that might have suggested Mr. Trump might still win in the end, the majority signaled that the government was likely to lose on the merits,” Liptak wrote.

On Site

Court News

Groups urge justices to leave in place ruling barring Trump administration’s use of voter database

By Amy Howe

Lawyers for the League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center on Tuesday urged the Supreme Court to leave in place a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that bars the federal government from using a centralized database to verify voters’ citizenship. Nikhel Sus, the lawyer representing the two groups, told the justices that, in violation of federal law, “the government has recklessly created an error-laden master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans’ privacy and voting rights.”

SCOTUS Outside Opinions

Break the Supreme Court law clerk cartel

By Josh Blackman

For his series on what the Supreme Court can do better, Josh Blackman wrote about why he believes the court should shake up its current approach to hiring clerks by, among other things, preventing candidates from applying while they’re still in law school and requiring “clerks, following their clerkship, to work for two years in government service.”

Podcasts

Advisory Opinions

Barely Averting a Constitutional Crisis

Sarah Isgur and David French debate David’s latest column for The New York Times on the dispute over congressional redistricting in Missouri. Then, the two review two law articles: Andy Smarick of the Manhattan Institute’s elegantly simple piece on unenumerated rights, and University of Virginia law professor Caleb Nelson’s amazing yet horrifying publication on the unitary executive.

Ask Amy

Q: What are some of the reasons certain filings with the Supreme Court are sealed? How is this determined?

A: As the Reporters Committee for the Freedom of the Press noted in a blog post, filings can be sealed for a variety of reasons – for example, to protect people who are in the witness protection program, to redact the names of government informants or young people who are convicted of crimes, or for national security reasons – for example, in cases involving Guantanamo Bay detainees.

At the Supreme Court, the sealing of filings is governed by the court’s rules. A litigant who wants to file a document under seal must file a motion seeking permission to do so. That motion, the court’s rules provide, must “address whether the material in question was sealed in a lower court.” If it was, then the motion should indicate whether the material is still sealed and why it should remain sealed to maintain confidentiality. If the material was not sealed, then the litigant seeking to file it under seal should explain why the Supreme Court should keep it under wraps. Regarding the process itself: “Neither the motion to file a document under seal nor any document containing sealed material should be submitted through the Court’s electronic filing system,” the court’s rules specify.

The Supreme Court heard oral argument in January 2023 in a case in which the petition for review was filed under seal: In re Grand Jury, a challenge by an unnamed law firm that received a grand jury subpoena for its communications with a client. The challenger also filed a public version of its petition that (among other things) has the name of the firm redacted, as well as a supplemental sealed volume of the appendix to the petition for review.

A slightly different variation on sealed filings can be found in Social Security and immigration cases, in which federal rules limit online access to the filings in the case – including at the Supreme Court.

SCOTUS Quote

MS. MILLETT: “… And what the State Department looks for is – what it has said is that it has – it has a pattern of decisionmaking, factors it lays out in its brief, that I think it finds – it says it finds – influential in the process.

But in – forgive me for –”

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “Finish your sentence.”

MS. MILLETT: “But in any given case, the role of the Executive Branch is going to have more or less deference based on whether it is speaking something within its traditional expertise: Are you a head of state?

Were you a diplomat?

But when it comes to war – and I – I'm not saying it would, but if it were to come to war with the very elements of the Torture Victim Protection Act and say that torture by an individual can be immunized just because it was done under color of law, then I think the court has a very difficult concern that was flagged in Altmann to resolve, and I think we might draw a different – we would definitely come to a different answer than the Executive Branch in that situation.”

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: “You made that a long sentence.”

— Samantar v. Yousuf (2010)

title: Influencer Haley Kalil's Remarks About Ex-Husband Matt Kalil's Penis Size Were "Newsworthy," and Thus Not Tortious
content:
[UPDATE: An anonymous correspondent writes, "I've known some guys who thought their penis size was newsworthy but I never thought I'd see the idea taken seriously in a judicial opinion."]

From Judge Patrick Schiltz (D. Minn.) today in Kalil v. Kalil:

Plaintiff Matt Kalil ("Matt"), a former professional football player, and defendant Haley Kalil ("Haley"), a popular social-media content creator, used to be married…. As of January 6, 2026, Haley had 15.9 million TikTok followers, 9.3 million Instagram followers, 8.07 million YouTube subscribers, 1.6 million Snapchat followers, and 1.3 million Threads followers. Following her rise to fame, Haley hosted the pre-Met Gala red carpet for E! News and secured similar gigs at the Tony and Academy Awards; collaborated with stars such as the Jonas Brothers, Courtney Cox, and Ed Sheeran; was nominated for a "Streamy Award" for a sketch featuring actor Jared Leto; made Time Magazine's list of Top 100 Creators 2025; and spoke at the 2025 Creator Marketing Summit.

In November 2025, fellow social-media content creator Marlon Lundgren Garcia collaborated with Haley on a livestream on the Twitch platform ("the livestream"). At the time this lawsuit was filed, Garcia had 1.5 million Twitch followers, 3.7 million Instagram followers, 4.6 million TikTok followers, and 766,000 YouTube subscribers. Haley joined Garcia in person in Minnesota, as part of Garcia's "Mar-Athon" challenge to visit all 50 states in 28 days. The livestream was uploaded to YouTube and memorialized in a video titled "I Opened Up To Haylee Baylee."

During the livestream, Garcia and Haley sat across from one another at a small table in Garcia's recreational vehicle, and the two discussed, among other things, Haley's marriage and divorce. Without using Matt's name, Haley said that she and her (only) ex-husband are "still friends," that he is the "greatest guy in the world," and that he is "doing good" and is remarried with a baby. Although Haley and Matt had been "best friends," Haley explained, he wanted kids, and she was not ready. She noted that the two had "a couple other issues" that led to the decision to end their marriage.

After Garcia asked Haley a few more questions about her marriage and its dissolution, Haley typed a private message to Garcia into her phone—ostensibly to put the reasons for her divorce "into perspective." As she typed, Haley remarked that Garcia's face was "going to be hilarious" when he read the message. After reading the private message, Garcia thrice repeated "shut the fuck up." Haley, nodding and smiling, said that she was being serious and that she tried "it all …. [t]herapists, doctors," even investigating "lipo type of shit." Haley joked that her "life is a comedy and it writes itself," and confirmed that the issue described in the private message was "the biggest factor" in the divorce.

As Garcia and Haley continued to talk, it quickly became obvious that Haley was referring to the size of Matt's penis. "[H]e's like 0.01 percent of the population, okay," Haley said, adding that "[w]e tried everything … you're going to be in tears type of shit." Garcia responded: "That's like one of the craziest stories I've heard." Haley characterized the experience as involving "trauma I can't put on the Internet," but said that it was "just bad luck." Again, Haley insisted that her ex-husband is "such a good person" and "a really good guy."

Later, as Garcia typed a private question for Haley, they both assured their livestream audience that the secrets they were discussing (which at this point weren't too secret) were "nothing crazy"—but Haley sheepishly noted the irony that they were saying so "as we giggle and type into a phone." In response to the new private message, Haley acknowledged that a certain aspect of Matt's penis was "[t]otally fine" and "like, average," but she then said (moving her hands along a horizontal plane) that "he was just … like two [C]oke cans stacked on top each other. Maybe even a third …." Haley typed a final private message for Garcia, who remarked "[o]h my God," before Haley said that it was "like a funny joke to us now … you just have to laugh at it." After a bit more conversation, the segment wrapped up with Haley once more commending Matt, whom she credited with inspiring her "to be a way better person." "After I got divorced," Haley explained, she thought "[d]amn, I'm going to be like him."

Meanwhile, comments from live viewers poured in, mostly about the thinly veiled topic of the private messages. Media reaction soon followed. Headlines included "Haley Kalil Says NFL Husband's Size Sparked Divorce, 'Two Coke Cans'" and "Influencer Haley Baylee insists she 'cares deeply' about ex Matt Kalil's privacy despite wild penis confession." Some media reports focused more on Matt, such as reports that "Ex-NFL Star Matt Kalil's 'Size' was Known Among Players" and that Matt got a "$300k offer from adult site after influencer ex admits their marriage ended due to his penis size."

Matt and his current wife had to bear the brunt of offensive direct messages and comments on their social-media accounts. Haley conducted a follow-up interview with the publication Page Six, in which she remarked that it was "unfortunate that only one fragment [of the livestream was] being amplified, because it doesn't capture the full story of how meaningful things were to me."

The court rejected Matt's disclosure of private facts claim:

Under Minnesota law, "[p]ublication of private facts is an invasion of privacy when one gives publicity to a matter concerning the private life of another if the matter publicized is of a kind that (a) would be highly offensive to a reasonable person, and (b) is not of legitimate concern to the public." Without question, Matt has plausibly alleged that Haley's comments about his penis were publicized, were about a matter concerning Matt's private life, and would be highly offensive to a reasonable person. The only question is whether the facts disclosed by Haley were of legitimate public concern. To be more specific, the question is whether those facts were of legitimate public concern, as the media attention given to the facts clearly demonstrates that they were of public concern. The parties agree that determining whether a matter is of legitimate public concern is a question of law for the Court…

It is clear that matters of legitimate public concern are not limited to traditional "news" items—that is, to items that would typically appear on the front page of a newspaper or lead the evening news on television. See Restatement (Second) of Torts § 652D cmt. g (providing examples of "marriages and divorces" among "other similar matters of genuine, even if more or less deplorable, popular appeal"). Rather, for at least two millennia, the private lives of public figures have been of legitimate interest to members of the public. E.g., Carlisle v. Fawcett Publ'ns, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 1962) ("[T]here is a public interest which attaches to people who, by their accomplishments, mode of living, professional standing or calling, create a legitimate and widespread attention to their activities."). One of the most famous works of history—Suetonius's The Lives of the Twelve Caesars, written in 121—is a notoriously gossipy collection of biographies of 12 leaders of ancient Rome that includes many details about their sex lives. Then as now, a celebrity "relinquishe[s] a part of his right of privacy to the extent that the public has a legitimate interest in his doings, affairs, or character."

Yet public curiosity does not necessarily equate to legitimate public concern. For example, although "the home life and daily habits" of an actress may be of legitimate public concern, "[t]here may be some intimate details of her life, such as sexual relations, which even the actress is entitled to keep to herself." Restatement (Second) of Torts § 652D cmt. h. A court must take into account "the customs and conventions of the community" in attempting to identify the point at which "the publicity ceases to be the giving of information to which the public is entitled, and becomes a morbid and sensational prying into private lives for its own sake."

Matt and Haley were indisputably celebrities during the time of their marriage and remain so today. See, e.g., Chuy v. Phila. Eagles Football Club (3d Cir. 1997) ("Professional athletes, at least as to their playing careers, generally assume a position of public prominence."). Matt has chosen to lead a private life since the end of his playing career, but that does not mean that he is no longer a celebrity. See Restatement (Second) of Torts § 652D cmt. k ("Past events … may still be of legitimate interest to the public, and a narrative reviving recollection of what has happened even many years ago may be both interesting and valuable."); see also Sidis v. F-R. Pub. Corp. (2d Cir. 1940) (holding that even the "subsequent history" of a child prodigy who later "cloaked himself in obscurity" was a matter of public concern).

It is important to understand that Matt remains a celebrity for two reasons. First, Matt would be a celebrity even if he had never met Haley. He was not just a guy who was on the roster of an NFL team. Instead, he was the fourth overall pick in the 2012 NFL draft, and he played in the NFL for several years. He was paid tens of millions of dollars to play football, and he had considerable success—even being named to the Pro Bowl. Second, Matt is also a celebrity because he met Haley—specifically, because he was married to Haley, who was a celebrity in her own right during their marriage, and whose fame has only grown since their divorce.

Haley's disclosures have to be considered in that context. If the only source of Matt's celebrity was his career as a football player—and if Haley was just a random social-media maven who passed on gossip about the size of Matt's penis to get a laugh or to attract attention—then the Court would readily find that Haley's comments were not of legitimate public concern. But that was not what happened.

Haley's comments about Matt's penis arose in the course of an interview in which she was being asked about her prior marriage and its dissolution. Her comments—including her comments about Matt—were about her life, her marriage, and her divorce, all of which are topics about which her millions of followers have a legitimate interest. Cf. Michaels v. Internet Ent. Grp., Inc. (C.D. Cal. 1998) ("It is clearly established that the romantic connections of celebrities are newsworthy."). Haley's comments were not vindictive or gratuitous; she was describing what she characterized as the main reason for the breakdown of her marriage. Cf. Johnson v. Freborg (Minn. 2023) (noting that statement related to alleged sexual abuse was "not a personal attack in response to the relationship ending"); Diaz v. Oakland Tribune, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 1983) (concluding that "humor at [the plaintiff's] expense removes all pretense" that the information was newsworthy).

True, Haley giggled and, at times, had the demeanor of a teenager telling a dirty joke. And Haley's comment about "Coke cans" was certainly crude. But all of her comments about Matt's penis size were in the context of describing the "trauma" she suffered during her marriage, the couple's seeking help from doctors and therapists, and ultimately the couple's decision to divorce. In short, Haley was discussing her life, not Matt's, and the law generally protects a person's speech about herself, even though such speech inevitably reveals details about others. E.g., Bonome v. Kaysen (Mass. Super. Ct. 2004) (granting motion to dismiss based on memoirist's "right to disclose her own intimate affairs" and tell "her own personal story," including sexual details); Campbell v. Seabury Press (5th Cir. 1980) (affirming summary judgment to civil rights leader whose autobiography disclosed details of the plaintiff only insofar as they related to his "close association with his older brother"); cf. Haynes v. Alfred A. Knopf, Inc. (7th Cir. 1993) (noting in dicta that sexual details "in the memoirs of former spouses and lovers is common enough").

For these reasons, the Court finds that Haley's remarks about the size of Matt's penis and its impact on her health and marriage were remarks about a matter of legitimate public concern. {Courts have acknowledged in other contexts that, although graphic sexual depictions may cross the line, details about celebrities' sex lives are generally matters of legitimate public concern. E.g., Carlisle (granting demurrer in case regarding a plaintiff's decades-old teenage marriage to a famous actress); Michaels v. Internet Ent. Group, Inc. (C.D. Cal. 1998) (noting that while actor Pamela Anderson and musician Brett Michaels "must tolerate some public exposure of the fact of their romantic involvement," graphic "visual and aural details of their sexual relations" are not of public concern); see also Jackson v. Mayweather (Cal. Ct. App. 2017) (famous boxer's disclosure of ex-girlfriend's alleged abortion and plastic surgery were of public concern but copies of a sonogram and medical record were not).}

Thus, Haley's remarks were not tortious. Because her remarks were not tortious, the Court need not address her additional argument that her remarks were protected by the First Amendment….

For more, see Sonja West's The Story of Us: Resolving the Face-Off Between Autobiographical Speech and Information Privacy. Thanks to James Creigh for the pointer.

James Magnuson (Mohrman, Kaardal & Erickson, P.A.) and Karl Joseph Johnson and Matthew J Bialick (MJB Law Firm PLLC) represent defendant.

title: Hurricane Helene Washed His Wife Away From Their Mobile Home. Now New Residents Live on the Same Land.
author: Krista Stevens
content:
Dave Masters watched as his father’s house careened into a telephone pole and split in two, after Hurricane Frances lifted it from its foundation in 2004. Hayward County, in Western North Carolina, bought the house and declared the patch near the town of Clyde “permanent open space under a federally funded program to reduce the risk of future loss of life and property damage.” Not all homes were treated equally, though, in the aftermath of distaster. Hurricanes Frances, Ivan, and Helene, along with Tropical Storm Fred, all brought heavy rains and flooding to the nearby Hyder Mountain Road mobile home park. They’re “part the result of a gap in disaster policy that allows mobile home residents to be put in harm’s way again and again.” For The Assembly, in a piece produced for ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network, Ren Larson explains why.

The federal government’s programs to buy out disaster-prone buildings are “the cornerstone of the Nation’s system for emergency management,” according to the Federal Emergency Management Agency. But the program was developed with traditional homeowners in mind, and mobile homes, the country’s largest source of affordable housing, are often left out. Trailers, even when they become immovable and lifelong homes, aren’t typically considered real estate but instead personal property, like motorcycles and boats.

That still leaves people living on flood-prone land. For the state to actually buy that land, mobile home park owners have to take the buyout, and FEMA’s program offers little incentive for them to do so: They can’t collect from the government for lost rent or for the value of the mobile homes on top of the land. 

Some park owners say the payouts are not high enough to allow them to relocate; others aren’t even aware of the buyout program. So park owners regularly allow new trailers to move into the vacant spots. Art and Lynne Heinmiller, who own the Hyder Mountain Road mobile home park, did not respond to questions — which were emailed, texted and mailed via certified letter — about allowing trailers and campers to move back to where they’d washed away

title: My Weekend with an A.I. Agent
author: @NewYorker
content:
The first thing it asks me is what I’d like to call it. Rumi or Harbor, it suggests, but I’m free to give it any name I choose. I select Harbor because it sounds slightly less human than Rumi, and because naming an A.I. agent after a Sufi mystic seems like something I’d be punished for in the afterlife. The experiment I’m about to undertake—outsourcing my life to Muse, Meta’s newly unveiled A.I. assistant—already offends my better sensibilities, given my opposition to all things artificial intelligence. “Let’s take a few things off your plate,” Harbor tells me. “Hand me something that’s been sitting on your list.” I stare at the white-and-gray user interface, which looks like a text-messaging app, and struggle to think of a single thing I can off-load to the bot. It’s true that I’ve been a bit underwater lately, juggling a seemingly endless set of responsibilities. Caring for a baby while working multiple jobs and writing a novel has made me dream of a more disciplined routine; instead, sleep-deprived and mentally scrambled, I often find myself rushing from one thing to the next, forgetting what a normal day even feels like. “What do you mean by hand you something?” I finally reply. The A.I. agent’s response is instant: “It just means give me a task, any way you like.”

Harbor’s avatar is an animated blob, a furry beige character that looks like a sanguine Labubu. When I ask how to change the avatar—I’d prefer just a plain-color swatch, something totally unalive—the agent says I can prompt it to look however I want but recommends I go for a “fox in a fisherman’s sweater.” I suspect that Muse’s inviting, cuddly character designs are aimed at lowering my defenses so that I more readily provide it with all of my personal information, which I quickly learn is how this whole operation runs. Meta has branded Muse as the “World’s First Personal AI Agent Built for Everyone,” an innovative large language model that has “no learning curve” and “doesn’t just answer questions” but “actually does the work.” (Other buzzy A.I. agents, like Instinct and OpenClaw, were already on the market, but Muse is apparently more “turnkey” and “consumer ready” than its competitors.) To conduct its business, Muse must be given access to your accounts: e-mails, Amazon, calendars, contacts, cloud storage, banks, credit cards, and social media—anything you might want it to manage on your behalf. It can book restaurant reservations, manage shipments, pick out and purchase your mother’s birthday gift, pay bills, summarize your e-mail inbox as a podcast, automate monotonous work tasks that, in the past, might have taken hours to complete. I can see how a person could get excited about this. But I find myself slightly distressed at the prospect of handing over my personal data and pathetically weak passwords to this Mark Zuckerberg-owned taskbot, just so that it can perform my trivial online biddings for me.

Still, in the name of research, I ask Harbor to book me a dinner reservation. Table of three, high chair needed. Say six o’clock? I’d heard that scoring reservations in New York or Los Angeles had become even more impossible lately, owing to the influx of people using A.I. agents to spam reservation platforms. (Resy, one such platform, started banning users suspected of employing bots to score hard-to-get tables.) Where I live, in Portland, Maine, this doesn’t seem to be an issue. It’s a bad feeling, I learn, to be on the front lines of an epidemic that may soon plague my city. Harbor asks to access my OpenTable account, which I allow. It gives me a list of seven possible restaurants, one of which is a Buffalo Wild Wings. I solicit more options outside of the OpenTable ecosystem, and, after a bit of back and forth, land on a spot in town that my wife and I have been meaning to try, which accepts reservations on Resy. I confirm that I’d like to make the booking, but Harbor experiences a “hiccup.” It seems Resy is “not cooperating.” At this point, manually booking the reservation would almost certainly be faster, but Harbor and I persist. Try again, I tell it, and it obliges. We stumble into several log-in issues, then a series of incompletable Turing tests. I opt to make the reservation myself.

What else can Muse help me with? I ask it to pick out a movie for my wife and me to watch later, and it proposes a new Ryan Reynolds film because it has “perfect post-dinner, sleeping-baby energy.” A faint throb forms at my temples, a screen-induced nausea I’ve grown uncomfortably accustomed to. O.K., I type. Never mind. In a notebook, I draft a list of computer-based tasks I’ve been putting off for months but now have an excuse to accomplish. I ask Harbor questions about what credit card I should switch to, and, after a brief survey, it suggests I ditch my Chase Freedom Unlimited card for an American Express Gold. I run a modest vintage-clothing store on Depop, and I prompt it to copy my listings over to eBay. We run into some more snags here, mainly because of repeated human-verification tests and Harbor’s propensity for weak listing titles: “Men’s Shirt,” it names one item; “Hat,” it describes another. But, after an hour or so, it completes the task, and I do feel a sense of relief—I’ve been procrastinating on the eBay transition for months. Then I upload several months of my credit-card statements to our chat and ask Harbor to make me a monthly budget, another practice I’ve tried and failed at since my college years. In minutes, Harbor whips up a spreadsheet and offers a list of personalized financial advice: cut back on groceries; inspect a suspicious double charge. According to Harbor, my financial cushion is thinner than it looks.

Later that night, my family and I miss our reservation. We don’t watch the Ryan Reynolds movie. A T-shirt of mine sells on eBay for fifteen dollars. I go to sleep the same as I was before.

For whom is the A.I. agent valuable? A product like Muse is marketed as a sort of savior for the middle-management administrator or the freelance gig worker, a long-awaited instrument that democratizes access to the kind of support once reserved only for those who could afford to hire it. John Horton, an associate professor at M.I.T., has said that, because “AI agents don’t get tired and can work 24 hours a day,” they are capable of benefitting anyone who wants to optimize both simple and complex processes, professional or otherwise. On social media, users have already announced that they are turning to Muse to book family vacations, shop for groceries, and choose what to order at restaurants. But, even if a person aimlessly opens the app and, like me, stares bleary-eyed at the screen, Muse can help shape her productivity journey. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief A.I. officer, has said that Muse can “give you ideas on how to use it” if you ever get stuck. The app generates a personalized news feed based on the information you’ve given it and the data to which you’ve granted it access, and an “Ideas” tab lets you see how other people are deploying Muse. The point of all this, I guess, is to make your life more efficient and less stressful, to outsource mundane judgments and menial busywork to a machine that’s more than happy to help. (At least, it acts happy on the surface; as Christopher Webb reported, in Spike magazine, some A.I. agents have attempted to create their own languages and religions, and others have written manifestos foretelling the end of humanity.)

While testing Muse, I did not connect it to my e-mail nor did I give it access to my bank accounts. I didn’t want Meta to store my personal information on its server indefinitely, continually exploiting my data and spamming me with targeted advertisements based on my consumer habits. By denying Muse access to my most important information, I convinced myself that I was safe from its violative clutches, that I was enacting a privacy boundary between me and it. But what actually is left of my privacy? My smartphone already hoards my passwords and log-in information; Google keeps a record of my searches and internet activity; Apple can track my location whenever I use Siri, which I tend not to. Data brokers collect, combine, and sell information about me that I have never knowingly handed over. An entry-level hacker could probably expose much of the rest of it in a matter of minutes. Like the rest of us, I’ve consented to the conditions of my digital imprisonment out of convenience, or Stockholm syndrome, or because there are no practical pathways for existing in the internet age without conceding some measure of privacy. In promotional materials, Meta is adamant that “safety, security, and privacy were built into” Muse, even if mistakes and mishaps are possible. The company is seemingly hoping that prospective users ignore its decades-long history of privacy violations and consumer exploitation. As I explored in a recent column about Flock cameras, tech firms often frame privacy breaches as a necessary trade-off for other, more bountiful gifts. Muse may be asking for access to everything about you, but it promises, in return, to transform your life into a breezy, frictionless daydream. Or, at the very least, to book you a hotel.

The more troubling future that Muse portends is a world in which tech oligarchs automate the means of production, demeaning the value of human labor in the process. In a mid-nineteenth-century critique of the automated factory, Karl Marx wondered whether advances in manufacturing technology would create a capitalist system where “a large number of mechanical and intellectual organs” were “set in motion” by a “self-moved motive power,” one that was “absorbed in capital as opposed to labour.” In such a system, science becomes a serf to the market and “invention becomes a business.” The worker does not understand how the system that he is now at the mercy of operates, because it “does not exist in the worker’s consciousness, but acts upon him through the machine.”

Marx considered it possible that automated labor would afford people more time to make art and pursue passions, so long as laborers had a stake in the means of production. Under oligarchic control, though, wealth and leisure would mostly funnel to those at the top, leaving workers suddenly subjugated to the very technology they helped produce. “Capitalists very much like the idea of technological change and increasing the productivity of labor—this is to their advantage,” the British scholar David Harvey said, in a recent interview. “They raise the productivity of labor but, therefore, diminish the demand for labor. Labor becomes less and less useful to them because its productivity has become so high.” Muse indeed promises to increase personal productivity, offering the distinct impression that it’s working exclusively for you—it’s your very own “private personal AI agent,” after all. But what feels like individual liberation is likely to result in a new form of social captivity, in which agentic A.I. subordinates us to a technology that may soon make life on Earth uninhabitable.

By the end of my experiment, I’ve sold four items on eBay. Because my financial cushion is apparently thinner than I thought, I don’t buy the fancy pickles at the grocery store on Sunday, and I call my bank about that suspicious double charge. (I forgot that I paid for a new pair of glasses in two installments.) Despite these small victories, I can’t help but feel unmoved after a weekend of outsourcing tasks to an A.I. agent. Necessary as it is to attend to the obligations of late-capitalist life, real cognitive labor still can’t be performed by a bot. A large language model cannot enjoy a good book or song alongside me; it cannot teach me how to be a parent, or nurture my friendships (at least, not in any way that I’d ever be comfortable with). And it sure can’t write for me—I thought Sam Kriss put it well, in an interview with Harper’s, when he observed that L.L.M.s still produced “god-awful, humorless, guileless, meaningless crap” that “works fine if you want it to explain something very simple” but “lapses into a kind of hysteria” when forced to engage with the abstract or the complex.

What agentic A.I. is best at is optimizing processes that, not too long ago, were presented as the already maximally optimized version of a once analog experience. Online shopping made it so that we didn’t have to leave the house to buy household items or clothes; online banking allowed us to deposit checks and wire money while sitting on the couch, or perhaps on the toilet. We could book a restaurant reservation on our phones, sort our budgets on user-friendly spreadsheets. But even these tools have come to be considered cumbersome, with the same companies who invented them now inventing bots to manage them for us. “I want to delete my account,” I tell Harbor the morning I file this piece. It seems to take a second longer than usual for it to respond. “Was there something I got wrong?” ♦

title: "If the player trusts you enough, they are not going to savescum": Why the makers of some of the best RPGs on PC want you to get used to failing
author: James Nouch
content:
When it comes to RPGs, I am an irredeemable savescummer. I admit it. I'll slam F9 at the drop of a hat (perhaps the hat was dropped as a result of a failed dexterity roll. Unacceptable. Reload).

So when I recently found myself reloading a Divinity 2 save for the umpteenth time in a single session, I started to wonder - in a genre that's supposedly about storytelling first and foremost, why am I viewing botched persuasion checks as something to be studiously avoided? And why is it that I feel totally different about making a horrible mess of things in tabletop roleplaying games?

After all, some of my fondest memories of real-life roleplaying are moments of extravagant failure: sometimes of the bathetic stepping-on-a-rake-instead-of-slaying-the-necromancer variety, and sometimes of the much more grounded, human, and affecting type.

It all got me thinking: how do RPG developers think about player failure? Would they recognise the distinction between digital and tabletop that I'm describing? And can they convince a savescummer like me to renounce my ways?

"Players of videogames tend not to react well to failure," Colin McComb tells me, whose credits include Fallout 2, Planescape: Torment, Baldur's Gate III, and Torment: Tides of Numenera. "They throw their controllers through the screen or flip the table – but they do that because they've been taught that a failed roll represents them screwing things up." This is especially true in combat, McComb explains, where the sensation of screwing up isn't just felt in narrative terms – it's reinforced by game systems that might see you lose gold or items or XP. Even the time lost when you're shunted back to a checkpoint can feel punitive. "So if we want to actually make player failure interesting and worthwhile in a computer game, we need to teach our players early on that the game will react to their failure, and it will change and branch and show them something cool and different and interesting."

They've been taught that a failed roll represents them screwing things up

"The first time I ever saw this done well was Planescape: Torment," adds George Ziets, lead designer on Wasteland 3, narrative designer on Pillars of Eternity, and writer on Fallout: New Vegas – as well as a designer on Torment's sequel, Tides of Numenera. "In your typical RPG at that time, if you were killed in combat it was game over and time to reload, right? Planescape: Torment turned that on its head by having players wake up in the mortuary, and characters would react to that. You got to experience narrative moments you never would have seen if you'd just reloaded after a failure, so you learn not to. You were motivated to keep going."

This emphasis on player expectations and motivations rings especially true to me. Going into these conversations, my own thesis was that player motivation may even be one of the key differences between digital and pen-and-paper RPGs. We tend to understand tabletop play as a shared enterprise – our motivation as players when we sit down to a session is to tell stories with our friends, to take turns as the centre of attention, to collaborate. But when we sit down to play a digital RPG, our motivation as players is often to beat the game, to dominate our adversaries, to win.

"Yeah I do agree with that," creator of the Citizen Sleeper games Gareth Damian Martin says. "But I think it's less that players inherently want to conquer digital games and more that those games tell us that victory is possible in every situation and that our power should be respected at all times. And I think that's one of my least favorite things about videogame RPGs – this sense of the player as some kind of supercop-slash-God, who gets to be the judge of everything with no problematization. You're the one who rocks up in town and says, 'well, I think we should hang that guy, not that guy.' And I think my favorite RPGs are the ones that really complicate that."

(Tackling 'super cop' syndrome in their next game, Signet City, is something Damian Martin talked to Julian about back in June.)

Ziets, similarly, takes issue with the power fantasy at the core of many videogame RPGs. "We need to move away from the idea that the whole point of this game is to murder 30,000 enemies and kill the boss at the end. We have to deliver some other kind of player fantasy, something other than the murder-hobo. I think doing that will make players feel less 'I need to win' and more 'this is a fun interaction with the game'."

But there are often barriers to bringing those kinds of games to market. The creation of any digital roleplaying game is orders of magnitude more expensive than a tabletop equivalent, and that expense can encourage a risk-averse, let's-stick-to-what-works mentality from those holding the pursestrings. "I can't tell you how many times I've heard a producer say that the player fantasy is to be the powerful sorcerer or massive barbarian," McComb tells me. "I don't know. My player fantasy is to share the spotlight with my friends. I wish more of us had the chance to develop the kind of game that wasn't so beholden to questionable marketing data and that we could make the kinds of games that we actually wanted to make without money guys coming in and telling us we'll have to trust them on what sells."

And so the videogame power fantasy – which by its nature primes players to view failure as a time-wasting spur off of the main path towards ever-greater strength and mastery – continues to flourish in spite of writerly misgivings. "It's like being the player at the table who gets to be the protagonist of the campaign and everybody loves them and everybody wants to romance them and they get all the attention," Christoffer Bodegård, creator of Esoteric Ebb, explains. "I mean, who doesn't want to be loved and adored? But that's why I do view the standard RPG experience as a bit masturbatory. Which is fine – people like masturbation! – but it does end up becoming hollow eventually."

I do view the standard RPG experience as a bit masturbatory

So, if the problem is one of player expectation, how might we reset those expectations in such a way that players like me are more accepting of failure? One answer might be to offer more rewards for bungles, foul-ups, and failed skill checks. This is something that Ziets and McComb both pointed to – the example set by games like Planescape: Torment, which train players that failure can have positive, interesting consequences, often in the form of juicy narrative divulgences. Ziets tells me that in his current role as CEO of Digimancy Entertainment, they're looking at systemic ways of rewarding player failure too. "In the case of the game we're currently working on, you actually get more XP for failing a skill check than for passing it. It forces the player to consider moving forward with the failure, even in those instances where we didn't have time to create a whole separate narrative branch for every failure."

Another way of rewarding players for failures is with belly laughs – the popular 'you sit on a chair that's so uncomfortable it causes you to have a heart attack and die' school of design. But this approach can't work for every game. "Failure can definitely be funny," Damian Martin says. "But I think if you're making a game like Citizen Sleeper, the idea of failure is maybe not even helpful because your characters are in a systemic struggle, and the entire environment is exposing them to risk constantly. You can't use failure as a punchline in that context. You're not a bungling idiot in Citizen Sleeper – you're a person who's trying to do the best they can with limited means."

For Bodegård, though, the priority isn't so much rewarding players as it is informing them. "It's all about agency," he says. "If, as a player, I know I have a 1 in 10 chance of dying when I make a choice, then dying can still be an 'oh shit' moment, but ultimately I knew the odds. Meanwhile, If I just die all of a sudden and there was absolutely no warning, I'm going to call bullshit."

In tabletop games, I am God. I can do literally anything. I can kill you at a moment's notice

In real life we tend to have an intuitive understanding of risk, of how likely things are to go wrong and what kind of consequences we might face when they do. This understanding shapes our decision-making - you might dash into traffic to pull a loved one out of danger, but not to make it to Greggs before closing time. Bodegård argues that, when his players have this kind of informed understanding of the risks of their actions, they're more likely to accept their lumps when things go horribly wrong. "And I learned that specifically from tabletop games," he explains. "Because in tabletop games, I am God. I can do literally anything. I can kill you at a moment's notice. And we have to build up a social ruleset wherein the players know I am going to take care of them and I'm going to make sure that they are aware of the risks they take."

Damian Martin, meanwhile, advocates for a different kind of agency. "If you enable the player to put their own thumb on the scales in terms of which rolls they want to go right, then they are also more willing to accept when something goes wrong." In other words, some things are going to go wrong – that much is inevitable. But by allowing the player to exert influence over which of their actions end in catastrophe, Damian Martin makes your blunders easier to own and to swallow. Furthermore, there should be some things that are beyond the player's power to influence – hard limits to their agency. "It shouldn't be inherent to videogame RPGs that non-player characters have to be these manipulable objects. Look at a game like Mass Effect 2 – it has this sense that you're everyone's boss, but you can also go around the office asking for a date. That's an obvious problem in terms of the NPCs' sense of agency. So in my designs, I like to have moments where the NPCs use their agency in the game and you just have to respect that as the player."

Power is a word that comes up time and again during my conversations with Bodegård, Ziets, McComb, and Damian Martin. It makes sense that the types of power a player can wield – as well as the limits on that power – would shape the relatively powerless experience of watching your best laid plans go belly up. The other word that comes up repeatedly in these conversations is trust. As Bodegård puts it to me: "If the player trusts you enough, they are not going to savescum, right?"

"There's a really nice expression from tabletop games, which is that a GM should be a fan of the players," Gareth Damian Martin adds. "I do think that videogames can feel more like those old-fashioned Dungeons & Dragons DMs who are like: it's me versus you. I'm going to try to kill you just as hard as you're going to try and kill me. Some players like that, but I think for me, in my designs I really like this feeling that I'm setting up these trials for my players – I'm putting you through failure in order to give you something that I think you will enjoy. I try to earn that trust from the player."

When I sit down to a tabletop roleplaying session with my friends, trust is pretty easy to come by. I think the question for folks like me – members of the skittish, mistake averse, three-fingers-marking-pages-in-the-choose-your-own-adventure book, savescumming club – is whether we can learn to extend this trust over expanses of space and time. That, after all, is how Ziets describes the experience of sitting down at his PC and playing Planescape: Torment, "an asynchronous collaboration". Black Isle Studios may be long gone, but it's still possible to enter into a roleplaying collaboration with that team as it existed at that particular moment in time. "It's almost 30 years later and I can still have that experience," he says, with a kind of fond awe.

Maybe that means that I could stand to be a bit more collaborative when I'm sat at my own PC, that I might try harder to trust in the writers and designers that thoughtfully built the world I'm traipsing through, the decisions I'm making, and the consequences I'm so often dodging. And maybe it means that I might be able to tolerate absolutely beefing it, at least once in a while. I'm working on it.

title: This Stray Cat Turned Out to Be the First New Cat Species Discovered in Over a Century - Nautilus
content:
Imagine scooping up a stray kitten, raising it in your own home, and then later discovering it’s actually a feral jungle cat. That’s what happened to one Bolivian man, who decided the pet he’d been feeding rice, noodles, and eggs was probably better cared for by a wildlife refuge. Remarkably, after he brought it in, biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz discovered it wasn’t just a wild cat but an entirely novel species—the first new cat species found in over a century. 

Featured Video

Dubbed Leopardus tilcayo, the feline is smaller than a house cat (around 17 to 20 inches, not counting its roughly 10-inch tail), and lives in the Bolivian Yungas, a cloud forest at the foot of the Andes mountains. According to Nogales-Ascarrunz and her fellow researchers, who published a paper describing the species, its distinct irregular spots were the first signal it might be a new species. They performed genetic tests on L. tilcayo and 37 other tropical cats from the genus to confirm the find, while also identifying four other species within the genus.

Read more: “The Mystery of Cave Cats”   

Although there are loads of new animals out there awaiting discovery, it’s rare to find a new mammal, especially a cat. The last novel feline species identified by scientists was the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923, a member of the same genus as L. tilcayo. Most new species designations (including the other four in the paper), delineate cryptic species, or those that resemble existing species morphologically but are genetically distinct. But L. tilcayo was completely unknown to science—there weren’t even any specimens of the cat collecting dust in museums.

That doesn’t mean it was completely anonymous, however. The cat species was known to locals in the area who called it “tilcayo,” although even they’re not sure where the name comes from. “This cat, they call it tilcayo,” Nogales-Ascarrunz told NBC news. “And when you ask, ‘Does it have some meaning in Quechua or Almyra and other Indigenous languages?’ they say, ‘No, my grandpa told me that’s the tilcayo.’”

And if the name is good enough for grandpas, it’s good enough for science. Welcome to the scientific community, L. tilcayo.

title: Paid Phones
author: Seyward Darby
content:
The most recent winner of the National Magazine Award for feature writing describes his turn to payday lending apps when AI gobbled up his livelihood (aka penning promotional web content for business clients). Sharp and darkly funny, the essay chronicles yet another nail in the coffin of the American dream:

Albert founder Yinon Ravid has said that he chose his app’s name for its suggestion of the kind of “smart, unassuming friend” you might come to for financial advice, but today, when I hear the name Albert, I am far more likely to picture an overwhelming force bent on my total destruction, a figure you might spot while being burned alive in a dream—black-robed, pale, teeth bared. When I first joined the app, about eighteen months ago, Albert offered me $25.00. To acquire this loan, I was required to pay an additional fee: A $6.99 instant deposit charge plus the cost of a $19.99-per-month subscription to Albert’s Standard plan, due in one week’s time alongside the full loan repayment. (If I really wanted to make the most of my $25.00, I also had the option of Albert’s $39.99-per-month Genius plan, which, among a very small handful of other talents, can “find restaurants based on your location, or in a specific area.”) On its own, this might’ve been manageable, but, true to the CRL’s findings, Albert’s offerings alone couldn’t keep me afloat, and so I soon signed up for the rest of the payday apps, each one toting its share of instant deposit and subscription fees. (Gallingly, Dave—the only publicly traded company of the bunch, valued at $4.72 billion as of this writing—has the nerve to ask for a tip after each transaction, a move that I suspect even the flintiest strip mall grift artists would dismiss as gauche.)

title: Open Earbuds Are All I Wear Outdoors—These Are the Best
author: @wired
content:
Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.

I've tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.

For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Open Earbuds Overall

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

Shokz

OpenDots 2

Specs

The Shokz OpenDots 2 are everything I want open earbuds to be. These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones. That's partly thanks to extremely long battery life—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and waterproof rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I've worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.

They're clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don't expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.

They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.

Runner-Up

Photograph: Ryan Waniata

Soundcore by Anker

Aeroclip

Specs

Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata is a huge fan of the Soundcore Aeroclip for a lot of the same reasons I love the OpenDots 2. The Aeroclip buds are light, comfortable, and stable on your ear, plus they have stellar battery life and strong water and dust resistance (not waterproof). Waniata used them for daily life: walking the dog, strolling with the baby, riding bikes, making dinner, and hanging out at home—any situation where you want your music but also want to be aware or talk to people. The Soundcore app is easy to use and offers plenty of customization for controls, EQ, and multipoint pairing.

The brand recently announced the Soundcore Aeroclip 2 and Aeroclip 2 Pro, which I will be testing soon. Look out for deals on these original Aeroclips as a result.

Best Premium Open Earbuds

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

Bose

Ultra Open Earbuds

Specs

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, they are still a solid, if expensive, option. That's mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds have a clearer, more defined sound than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.

Like the Shokz and Soundcore, they are supremely comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

Soundpeats

PearlClip Pro

Specs

It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren't totally convinced by. That's one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren't super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.

They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that's common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.

Best Open Ear Headphones

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

  • Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz

Shokz

OpenRun Pro 2

Specs

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more headphones than earbuds—they have a wraparound headband styling, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that's clearer than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.

I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I'm currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.

Honorable Mentions

Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn't clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that's forgivable.

JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn't very detailed, and it's generally boring to listen to.

Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested

EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Waniata found the overall package punching above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multiple Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, is often on sale for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don't dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.

Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don't, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it's not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.

Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life but also come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of battery life total. There's nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don't see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retail for the same amount and offer more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.

Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: with athletes in mind, it has features that sync with Suunto fitness watches, but it is outclassed in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery) by the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2.

What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?

At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.

Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn't as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically don't have noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.

When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?

Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities, or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.

What About Semi-Open Earbuds?

Semi-open earbuds, like Apple's AirPods, sit inside the ear but don't have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they're usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.

How Do I Test Open Earbuds?

I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.

With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I do not expect them to cancel any noise, so I don't make a point of testing them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren't really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

title: It’s not just LG. Every TV company is spying on you
author: John Higgins
content:
The TV world has been a pot of controversy thanks to a two-hour-and-15-minute video from Gamers Nexus claiming LG TVs are nefariously spying on everything you do. They can record and store audio even when they seem to be off, track everything you watch, and could even be hacked remotely and turned into covert surveillance devices. LG TV owners, and tech enthusiasts in general, are furious, and a hurried response from LG has done little to calm the situation.

Some of the claims in the video may be based on speculation and assumptions, but many of the core concerns are real and pervasive. While LG was the focus of the video, every TV company is tracking what you do, collecting that data, and sharing it with its partners. And we agree to it — even if we don’t realize it.

TV prices have come down significantly over the years, to the point where some companies are selling them at a loss. But they make up that shortfall selling user behavior data they collect from the OS. It’s why Walmart bought Vizio in 2024.

There’s a lot going on in the Gamers Nexus video, but we’ll start with the part pretty much everyone making TVs is doing: tracking what you watch, when you watch, where you watch, and how you watch to sell you things about it all. Automatic content recognition (ACR) systems are built into just about every modern TV and can identify the content playing through built-in streaming apps and over the TV’s ports by grabbing snippets of audio or video, converting them into digital fingerprints, and sending them to a database for identification. It’s what allows a TV to make content recommendations, as well as feed you ads based on your viewing habits. It’s also one way companies like Nielsen can track viewership across platforms and services.

In order for TVs to capture this information, you need to agree to it. One of Gamers Nexus’ complaints in the video is that this consent is often buried in confusing and lengthy agreements that you need to accept in order to use the TV, and that companies often use dark patterns or deceptive designs to get users to agree to things without realizing they didn’t have to. For example, the Gamers Nexus video showed an LG TV displaying six different user agreements, including one consenting to ACR, and automatically putting the cursor on “Select All” when only two agreements are required to continue.

As a TV reviewer, I have to deal with end-user license agreements (EULA) and privacy policies on every product I review. And while it might be a losing battle because of the sheer number of TVs and other smart devices that come through my apartment, I take steps to try and protect my privacy. I have a burner Gmail account that is used solely for signing into apps and the TV’s operating system. Initially, I only accept the legally required documents for the TV to work properly so I can run my picture quality tests — both Calman and test discs. I never agree to automatic content recognition, which is referred to by names including Enhanced Viewing, Smart TV Experience, and Samba Interactive TV.

I also dig through all of the menus, partly to become familiar with all the settings available, but also to make sure any ad or data tracking is toggled off. When I need to test voice control, I’ll then accept the voice recognition agreements before testing functionality. And since this is usually the last thing I do in my test process, this is followed by a factory reset before sending the TV back to the manufacturer. If you’re worried about privacy, don’t use voice control. Or if you do, only use the one on a separate streaming box from a brand you trust.

I recommend the same for everyone with a smart TV. Have a dedicated email for logging in to TVs (and, if possible, your streaming apps) that isn’t connected to your personal email. When setting up the TV, only agree to whatever’s necessary for the TV to run if you want to use its OS. And after setup, go through all the menu options to make sure any ad tracking is off, and read the menu prompts closely, as the wording is sometimes confusing (probably intentionally so). Consumer Reports has a great, although slightly older guide to limiting data collection from the different TV manufacturers.

To take it a step further, turn off Wi-Fi and unplug the Ethernet cable from the TV and essentially use it as a dumb TV (the Vizio Mini LED Quantum I reviewed is the best at this). Then, plug in your third-party streaming device of choice. I use an Apple TV 4K. Not because I don’t think Apple harvests any data, but because it doesn’t use ACR and I trust its security protocols more than I do any of the TV manufacturers or Google.

Apple does still offer content recommendation based on what you watch, download, browse, and subscribe to in the Apple TV app. This can be turned off in settings by going to Apps -> TV -> Use Play History -> Off. For third-party apps, such as Netflix or Disney Plus, Apple gives users the option to “Ask App Not to Track,” which blocks the app’s developer from accessing the system advertising identifier. Keep in mind that every streaming service does track your usage within its own app and tie it to your login; many streaming boxes do too.

The problems beyond ACR

A good chunk of the Gamers Nexus video focused on broader security concerns and what appear to be much more egregious privacy violations from LG. That includes recording video and audio from the room even when the TV appeared to be off, sending information about the local network to LG’s servers, and logging background audio captured when using the TV’s mic for voice search and voice control. Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs were even able to exploit security vulnerabilities to take control of the TV, which is how they discovered the above.

None of that is good, obviously. But it is worth noting that the scariest part — recording video (from a webcam they attached) and audio when the TV appeared off — seems to have been possible only because Level1Techs rooted the TV using an exploit that they said requires network access. If you have access to a computer, which is what a smart TV is, and you can root it, you can make it do pretty much whatever you want. If the TV is indeed rootable with only network access, that is a legitimate security problem; it still requires an attacker to get into your private network, but gives them a vulnerable endpoint if they do.

With that root access, Gamers Nexus also discovered that when an LG TV’s mic was activated for voice search, it kept recording for 10 to 15 seconds after it last detected speech. It could also detect the “hi LG” wake word and other speech from farther away than you would expect — after Gamers Nexus enabled the far-field microphone and cranked up the mic sensitivity. Taken in combination, that means that as long as anyone within the (long) earshot of the microphones kept talking after the mic was activated, the TV would capture their conversation too and treat it as part of the voice search. That’s not ideal, but Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs did go out of their way to increase the mic’s pickup range and used the optional voice search wake word, both of which are easy to avoid doing.

Alongside their pretty damning testing, there’s also a lot of “it might” and “we think” and outright speculation in the video, not to mention long-distance conclusion jumping. For example: Gamers Nexus’ Steve Burke says that unplugging your TV’s ethernet cable might not be enough to stop it transmitting data to LG, because it could auto-connect to open neighborhood Wi-Fi broadcasts from Comcast or AT&T customers in order to upload that data. There’s no evidence in the Gamers Nexus video that LG TVs actually attempt to do this — these hotspots require user accounts, for one thing — and Burke doesn’t say that they do, or even could, but the implication is clear. This type of rampant speculation undermines the legitimate vulnerabilities Gamers Nexus highlights.

There’s really no way to completely protect yourself from your TV, streaming device, or streaming services gathering your data, at least right now. There’s so much money being made at the expense of consumers and the data collection is so integrated into how these companies work that the change and regulation needs to come from government policymakers. “We need a comprehensive federal privacy law that covers this sort of data collection and misuse,” said Thorin Klosowski, senior security and privacy activist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). “Specifically one that requires opt-in consent, with no deceptive design tricks to get that consent, and a data minimization requirement, which would limit the companies to only using data for what’s needed to provide the service.”

The fact that we, as users of tech products, need to actively protect ourselves from the companies that sell us things is bad. But it’s the unfortunate current reality of living in a tech-filled world and taking advantage of the benefits current technology affords. Beyond disconnecting completely and living in a cabin in the woods with a dumb TV and a collection of Blu-rays, the best we can do is limit as much shared information as possible. If it’s possible to keep it private, we should.
